summary:
On 1 September 2025 the Transitional Legislative Assembly of Burkina Faso passed a law criminalising consensual same-sex relations, carrying two to five years' imprisonment plus fines. The law passed unanimously in the unelected 71-member transitional parliament and took effect immediately. Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala stated that prison terms of between two and five years, as well as fines, apply to perpetrators of "homosexual or similar practices", and that foreign nationals who violate the law will be deported.

The criminal prohibition is carried by a revised Personal and Family Code (CPF) approved by the junta's council in July 2024 as part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law, and the code entered into force on 1 September 2025. Homosexuality had never before been outlawed in Burkina Faso; the ban took effect as criminal-code law on 1 September 2025. The criminal code in force since that date bans homosexual acts and the promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour.

The law was enacted amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space. The military junta has held power since September 2022. France 24–AFP coverage of 22 September 2025 described fears of a witch hunt and increased self-censorship in the LGBTQ community; as of 28 September 2025 no arrests under the law had been reported.

Same-sex activity was legal before 2025, with an equal age of consent implemented in 1996 and overturned by the 2025 code. The Constitution's Article 23 defines marriage as the free consent of a man and a woman, describes the family as the basic unit of society owed state protection, and does not authorise same-sex marriage. That article bars discrimination in marriage based on race, colour, religion, ethnicity, caste, social origin or wealth, a list that omits sexual orientation and gender identity. Pre-existing prohibitions on same-sex marriage and same-sex adoption remain in force.

Under the U.S. Department of State's reporting, only married, cohabiting heterosexual couples married at least five years may adopt, and single applicants are almost never permitted to adopt.

The 2011 Human Rights Report found the law did not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation in employment and occupation, housing, statelessness, access to education or health care, while societal discrimination on those grounds persisted. LGBT persons were reported as occasional victims of verbal and physical abuse; religious and traditional beliefs did not accept homosexuality; and there were no reports that the government responded to societal violence and discrimination against them. LGBTQ organisations had no legal presence in the country but existed unofficially, with no reported violence against them.

National adult HIV prevalence stands at 0.80% of those aged 15 to 49. Of an estimated 94,000 adults living with HIV, 65% have antiretroviral drugs, and 28% of children aged 0 to 14 do, against all-ages coverage of 32% in 2010.
tangentialFactors:
Burkina Faso joined the roughly 22 of 54 African states that disallow same-sex relations when the ban took effect, per Africanews' July 2024 reporting.

The criminalisation arrived within a broader junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil society, which shapes how the law is likely to be enforced and how openly it may be contested.

France 24–AFP reported on 22 September 2025 that the law had produced fears of a witch hunt and increased self-censorship among LGBTQ people, even before any arrests were documented.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents arrests, prosecutions or convictions under the new law; as of 28 September 2025 no arrests had been reported, and later enforcement activity is unresolved.

Whether the deportation threat announced by Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala has been carried out against any foreign national is not sourced here.

The inventory does not address legal gender recognition, identity-document marker rules, or any screening regime that could expose a trans visitor's status at entry; those questions remain unresolved on this record.

Whether the 2011 Human Rights Report's findings on employment, housing and health-care non-discrimination remain accurate after the 2025 code is not sourced.
